title: Pensacola Jazzers and absorbing Lee Collins's players
summary: In Pensacola the band became the Pensacola Jazzers; Joe Wynn took Al Morgan and Edmund Hall from the Lee Collins group, forming a seven-piece band.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: And, uh, where did you go after this band, you know what I mean?

Well, after, like I said, we went out to Florida, in Pensacola, Florida, we stayed out there about a year and nine months. Mm-hmm. And, uh, the band, we got out there, the people gave us a name, they started calling us the Pensacola Jazzers.
Yeah, yeah.
You see, but, uh, there was another player, a fellow had an undertaker named Prince Morris.
Mm-hmm.
And he had hired a band, they was already out there, that was Lee Collins.
Oh, yeah.
It was a Lee Collins group, and he had, uh, Lee Collins on trumpet, he had, uh, uh, uh, what was his brother? You see, it was Percy Willie and...
What?
Oh, yeah, well, yeah. Oil on trombone.
Yeah.
And, uh, Evan Hall on clarinet. Mm-hmm. Al Morgan on bass. Mm-hmm. And I believe he had Joe Strada on drums, yeah. And had a very fine banjo player in those days named Caffrey.
Oh, yeah, yeah.
Yeah. So, uh...
And they were playing at the same time as you and Pennsylvania.
Yeah, they were playing with a fellow named Prince Morris.
Mm-hmm.

So, uh, they had some trouble about their money with Prince Morris, and this fellow, Joe Wynn, he, uh, he took Al Morgan and, and, uh, Edmund Hall out of that band. Oh, yeah. See, and put them with us. Yeah. Then we had another, we got another woman piano player named Helen Jackson.
Yeah.
She was originally from there. But his first piano player was named Beck. Come back to me now. She was named Beck.
Oh, yeah.
And the one that, uh, when they made the change, in other words, the lawyers in the band, that's why we picked up Al Morgan, Edmund Hall, and picked up a piano player named Helen Jackson.
Mm-hmm.
That was the band that consisted, so, uh...
That was your seven-piece band?
Yeah. So, uh, we took, uh, Hall at, uh, bought him a sax. He wasn't playing sax then.
Edmund Hall?
Yeah.
Yeah.

And bought him, I think he bought him a C-melody brass sax, I remember well. And, um, well, he couldn't read so much, but Edmund Washington could read, so what we'd do, we'd buy numbers, like, stock numbers, and run them down. Well, Edmund Hall had such a good year, you know. He'd play, uh, he'd learn to lead, and then Edmund Washington would play and play, and maybe the other part, maybe the third hour to the part, see, something like that, see. And then he would double on, climb out on certain numbers, you see, because we had one number that was real famous, uh, uh, for us, uh, let's see, what the name of that thing, uh, uh, uh, uh, it'll never come to me later. But anyhow, the number that we played was just like, I said we played then, like we had, that was a tiger leg, you had, uh, Buckley got a hole in it. And then I remember, uh, a number of pop tunes came out there, uh, I can't see, but anyhow, that was in, like I said, 24. All the numbers that came out, like, in stock, we'd buy them, because that was the trend then, you know, and then we'd keep up like, you know, all these blues and things like that, the people liked that, you know. And, uh...
And when did you go after this band broke up?

Well, as I said, we, we, in Pensacola, we were working for these people, and so, uh, we used to play a town like, like Mobile, and go to Montgomery, and, uh, there's a couple other times we'd go. So, uh, around about, uh, let's see, close to 26, well, we left Pensacola, no, we made a trip down to Florida, that's what we made, a trip all over from Pensacola to, uh, Jacksonville, Florida.
